posts.author: Lord Vectra
posts.body:
Nope. This would fall under AI-assisted. I use Copilot a lot myself. I use it as a debugger myself or as a tool to speed something up.
For a quick example: Each Event method (Control Switches, Add Items, Change Level, etc) each has a number attached to them. I was making an event log script (extension of a Crash Log script I made), and I needed them in a list with their corresponding number (so RMXP knew what to write). However, I'm not a masochist, so I had Copilot make the list for me.
It also helps optimize scripts which, I think, is the most important function for Game Devs. In my leveling script, there was a specific part that lagged like CRAZY! I didn't know why, and I tried so many things. Plugged it into Copilot, told it what the issue was, and it ended up finding the issue within a few minutes. I asked it to explain why it worked and now I know.
And my skills as a coder did refine itself by plugging my scripts into Copilot and asking "Can this be smaller or more optimized?" Scripts I make now are definitely significantly smaller than when I started.
rpgLord69 said:
Around half a year ago I asked AI to explain to me about javascript prototypes and what is PIXI and how the draw order works etc. Of course that gave me advantage vs. someone who didn't have AI.

I will say it also helped me learn Ruby quite quickly. Some coders gave me some flack, but I learned a lot by just giving it scripts and asking it to tell me what the code does and why, word-by-word/line-by-line. In a very short amount of time, I can just make scripts myself without Copilot (tho I still use it for optimization so I can compare).
ANYWHO, its AI-assisted as everyone else already said. AI-assistance has been around way before it became the world craze that it is now.

ANYWHO, what you do with it is AI-assisted. I would recommend, however,
if your issue is crash logs
(which is essentially what you're complaining about), I'd recommend making a script that gives you a backtrace.
Basically, the program will give you the error that caused the crash but if you open your crash log, it'll tell you what ran before it which would allow you to catch cases where the error-causer is actually elsewhere. Ruby can create files, so imma assume your program can too.
I made one because some of the scripts are really long and interact with each other, so the crash log tells me what was running before the crash as well which allows me to backtrack. For example, I had a crash when you loaded a game (New Game worked fine). Come to find out, it was because I put things in the wrong order elsewhere when the program kept telling me it was in some other area unrelated to what actually caused it.

Short Answer: I can explain the backtrace, but without your game and no Java knowledge, I'd unfortunately be a terrible fixer for you lol
Rest of the answer: But to help, that's already the backtrace it seems (the format just confused me). The number on the far right is the line of that plugin that is being called but it works top to bottom (Each line called the line above it). I dont know if you know what a backtrace is so I'll just explain:
When an error pops up, it logs where the error was detected, and then it logs whatever called the method that caused the error, then it logs whatever called that method, and it goes all the way back to beginning of the call-chain.
So if we have method A, B, C, D, and E. If A calls B which calls C and C is when the error is detected, the backtrace would show C and then what in Method B called C and what in Method A called B.
So you'll see something like:
C [error] line 123
B line 123
A line 123
Now, the unfortunate part is you'll need to look at each line and use context to what the issue is (so it does require a hint of coding knowledge to fix even if you find the issue).
Thats why, in my game, I have the crash log tell me the map of the player, their coordinates, and scripts being ran at the time of the crash, then I have a separate log that shows the last event they activated (because that didn't show up on my crash log so any call script errors were invisible).

After re-reading, although it's a bit late for this situation since you found the problem, a bit of advice I'd give is, if a specific line keeps getting an error, if you know how to make the game create files via Javascript, you can ask it to output to a file prior to that line being called (I use .txt files). It's something I do that's been helpful.
For example, I'd get an nil error from a method so I would go in and ask it to give me a series of things so I can see which is nil. Then you take that code and import it higher in the chain until you find the moment it goes nil (or if its nil the entire way).
I plan to do one for my battle system (damage calculation specificlally) because the coding is getting extremely robust, so Imma have a txt file that exports the damage after each step, so in the event the damage goes haywire, I can simply go to it and see what happened.
I don't know your plugin so im just giving advice that may help you in the future if you haven't thought of it already.
